newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Greece vows to block Turkey's acceptance to EU.
newsitem.headline: Greece vows to block Turkey's acceptance to EU.

text.p: Greece vowed on Saturday to block Turkey's application for European Union membership as long as the division of Cyprus remained unsolved and Ankara continued its "aggression" over the Aegean.

"If there is no solution to the Cyprus problem, if Turkey does not stop its aggressive policy on the Aegean and if it does not respect human rights Greece cannot consent to the evolution of relations between Turkey and Europe," Greek Deputy Foreign Minister Yannos Kranidiotis told a news conference in Nicosia.
Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since 1974 when troops from Turkey invaded the north of the island after a brief coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.

"We would be willing to help the (application) process of Turkey to Europe if it complies with these terms, these preconditions which are political preconditions. Our problem with Turkey is a political problem," Kranidiotis said at the conference with Cypriot Foreign Minister Yiannakis Cassoulides.

Kranidiotis said it was in the interests of Turkey, and Turkish Cypriots living in the island's north, for Ankara to "make concessions related to Cyprus". He urged Greece's European partners to pressure Turkey to do so.

Greece, the closest ally of the Greek Cypriots, who are recognised as the only legitimate government of the island, came to the brink of war with Turkey over a deserted Aegean islet in 1996. A clash was averted with last-minute U.S. intervention.
Some 30,000 Turkish troops are in northern Cyprus, declared a Turkish Cypriot state in 1983 but recognised only by Ankara.

The United Nations and mediators have been trying for decades to reunite Cyprus under a federal system without success. The U.N. is now trying to arrange talks by June between President Glafcos Clerides, as head of the Greek Cypriot community, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.
It would be their first encounter in nearly three years.
This latest burst of diplomatic activity has been spurred by Cypriot hopes of joining the European Union. Membership talks would be greatly eased if the division of the island were ended.
The U.N. mission on the island has been holding talks with the two sides to prepare for the meeting and convince them of the need for goodwill gestures to improve the climate for talks.
Relations between the two sides, though never cordial since 1974, suffered a serious setback last summer after several killings on the ceasefire line partitioning the island.
Former South Korean Foreign Minister Han Sung-joo, special representative of the U.N. secretary-general on Cyprus, was due in Cyprus on Saturday for talks with the two leaders.
